utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will give its decision on the Prosecution's motion filed on the 20th of June to exclude the testimony of Witness T-42. The Prosecution contends that the witness will testify about an attack on Bosnian Serbs -- on the Bosnian Serb-held Ilidza in April 1992 which led to the establishment of a hospital in Blazuj. He came to direct that hospital. They contend that the -- Blazuj is a full 10 kilometres or more from the Sarajevo city centre and at least 3 full kilometres outside the confrontation lines. The only part of the witness's evidence which, in the Prosecution's view, might fall within the indictment is that section that relates solely to the operation of the hospital in Blazuj. In their submission, this does not in any way relate to the potential criminal liability of the accused. It is on these bases that they seek the exclusion of this witness's evidence. The Defence in reply make a number of arguments. I will outline some of them. They say that the witness is an eye-witness to military activities taking place in the Ilidza municipality and its surroundings. He's also an eye-witness to consequences of those activities for the civilian population and the military personnel deployed in that territory from the 22nd of April until the end of the conflict. They make the point that on the basis of the evidence led by the Prosecutor, Ilidza is a part of the city of Sarajevo. They also contend that the Prosecutor has characterised those military activities as a campaign of shelling and sniping against civilians. The Defence say they contest that qualification and submit that the intensity of military activities of the ABiH indicate that it was not the civilian population of the ABiH that was the objective of the military of the SRK. A weakness in this submission, I might say, is that it doesn't say how the witness's evidence would help the Chamber in this issue. But they go on to say that Witness T-42 will testify on all aspects of the Zica Hospital's daily running where he was the director during the armed conflict in the city of Sarajevo, in particular, he will testify on the military status of patients and on the nature of their wounds and, importantly, the geographical location of the hospital, surrounded by hills controlled by the ABiH. The Chamber takes the view that these submissions provide enough information to warrant hearing this witness and although some of the evidence will relate to the pre-indictment period, 1992, and to an area which is some 3 miles from the Sarajevo theatre, the Chamber takes the view that the submissions warrant hearing this witness. It will, therefore, dismiss the Prosecution's motion. The dismissal of this motion, of course, does not mean that the witness can testify on any and everything. The Chamber still, of course, has the duty to see that his evidence is at all times relevant. A worrying aspect of this submission I should say is the lateness of the Prosecution's motion, coming as it did just one day before the witness was scheduled to testify. The Chamber finds that this is not an acceptable procedure. That's the Chamber's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will assign one hour for each party. I hope you heard that, Mr. Tapuskovic. One hour for each party to lead evidence and for the cross-examination. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has a pseudonym as well as voice and image distortion. Could this document be please shown to him so that he can confirm that it is his identity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I would like to have this document tendered as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D253, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we could move into private session now so that the witness can introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, since our time is very limited, we need to deal with just with the most important things. So please take care just to answer me when the typing on the screen, on the transcript, stops; when you see that, that means that it's the end of my question. When you see that the cursor has stopped, then you can begin your answer. So my question is: Did you join the Army of Republika Srpska; and if you did, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to cover things more quickly, I would like to show you a map, 65 ter number 2872. While we're waiting for the map to appear, can you please tell us if you know when the lines were set up, the lines of separation, between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that area where you were at that point in time when you joined the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to Dobrinja I for the first time, the line was already established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the map now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I could deal with this in cross, but rather than do that, maybe it would assist everyone if we could have some specification of what year we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Witness, what year is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought the witness already said that. I mean, it's something that is not implied, but all right, very well. Can we now zoom-in on the southern section of the map where Dobrinja is. Can we scroll down a little bit more -- actually, scroll up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The line of separation that you said existed in May 1992, can you mark it here on this map as being the line where you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, this is 1992. How does this witness's evidence relate to the issues in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness remained at the line throughout the war. In order to speak about anything that has to do with the conflict, also during the time-period from August until the end of the war, he needs to show us the lines first, the ones that existed at the time, and how the lines were established, what happened. In order for me to be able to ask him about anything that has to do with his activities at the beginning of the war, he lived there in a location that he will indicate to you, and as a person who was born there and lived there, he must show you what happened so that he went to the lines and stayed there until the conflict was over. It will be hard for him to explain to you anything further if he cannot say first something about the lines of separation that he went to at the end of May 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Bring him to the period covered by the indictment as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I would like to do that in view of the time that I have, but I think it's difficult to question any witness unless he first explains how he became a soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will do it if you just get on with the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please indicate the place where your house was before you went to join the lines that you marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that you made any kind of mark. Can you please mark that with a letter C.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where is that railway station where you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The station is at Ilidza, it's in this direction, but you cannot see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom-in a little bit more to the right of that map so that we can see that? Very well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any case in that direction. How far was that from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think I can give you an approximate distance. It was about 6, 7, or 8 kilometres, up to 10 at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And for how long were you able to go to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was able to go to work until the end of March. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happens so that you couldn't go to work anymore, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't able to go to work because it wasn't safe to pass through any more. There were many events that had already happened in Sarajevo, and because of everything that had happened that we were able to follow on the media, they didn't allow for a sensible person to embark on going to a part of town controlled by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about when the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The Yugoslav People's Army withdrew sometime in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you monitor that withdrawal? What did that mean? How did they withdraw? What was the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm questioning how the witness is in a position to comment anything about the significance of the withdrawal of the JNA from regions in and around Sarajevo in 1992 and how the withdrawal of the JNA at that period of time is actually relevant to the case that we're here for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this information, even assuming that the witness is in a position to provide it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we look at any count in the indictment, or if we start again from Count 7 and move from there, we know that what is being discussed here -- continuously discussed here -- I mean, if this is something that has to be excluded, then I would very gladly just leave that out and then start from September, or rather, August 1995. The whole indictment speaks about the transformation of the Yugoslav People's Army into the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The entire indictment speaks about the fact that all the weapons of the JNA remained in the position -- in the possession of the Army of Republika Srpska. The entire indictment says that the JNA took up all the important strategic positions before 1995 and the Serbian Democratic Party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop. Witness, are you in a position to -- to tell us what was the significance of the JNA's withdrawal in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that the army withdrew and that I saw all of that and I lived there that in the area where I was born, and had they not left some heavy weapons for us, vast quantities of -- and that it did not leave any vast quantities of heavy weapons behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Next question. I'm hearing the witness's language, B/C/S, in the translation. Can I ask the court usher to look at it for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us, for example, that place where your house was or in that area generally, did you see any of those heavy weapons thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I lived, that's where I saw when they pulled out of the airport. I saw three tanks which went to the south behind our neighbourhood, our settlement, and I saw four Pragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where were the four Pragas in the beginning? Can you please mark that with the letter P.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us this place where your house is, what is the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole area is called Kotorac, and the place above is called Gradac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe that elevation and tell us how high it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The elevation or Vrh, it's about 600 metres high and it is in the shape of a pyramid. The actual peak of the elevation is not so big. It's inaccessible. The only way you can reach it is on foot. And then there is a drop below like 2 or 300 metres lower than that it turns into a kind of mild hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the nearest hill in the direction of the north?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the north the closest hill is Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate where Mojmilo is and what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Gradac is just a few square metres wide where -- at the highest point of the elevation, but can you please describe the characteristics of Mojmilo in terms of the height characteristics of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mojmilo is the same height all along its length, from Nedzarici to Dobrinja to Vrace and I think that it is much higher -- well, not that much higher but it's higher than the Gradac elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That hill is on that side, but is there any hill here to the west?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to the west it's not a hill, it's the mountain, Mount Igman, that dominates the whole area. It is more than a thousand metres high. I don't know its exact height, but it's over 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how far is that from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mojmilo hill is 2 and a half to 3 kilometres as the crow flies -- well, in fact, as the crow flies and as you drive and Igman is approximately the same distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, did anything stick in your mind in the early days regarding the combat activities where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was your father wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, my submission is that that's outside of the indictment period and whether or not his father was wounded outside the indictment period is not relevant to the charges in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. Move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in general, could you please tell us. As regards combat in any period, including the period relevant for the indictment, where was the fire coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim forces opened fire from Mount Igman, from Hrasnica, from Kobac, from Mojmilo, and they mostly opened artillery fire. In that area where my house was, where I was born and where I lived, my father was wounded, a lot of civilians were killed, and a number of them were seriously wounded. So these were the directions that I mentioned, in particular in 1992, in the summer of 1992, there was constant fire, barrage fire, on the civilian areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But let us move on to the period relevant for the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was going to raise my objection with respect to the period -- the mention of the period of the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, please bear in mind that 45 minutes have been allocated for each party in this -- in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am keeping an eye on the time, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know at all when General Dragomir Milosevic was appointed the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exact -- the exact date, but it was in 1994, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How was it in 1994 in the area where you were, where you lived with your family and with your neighbours and -- the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, 1994, let me describe what the situation was in the area where I and my family lived. The beginning of the year was quite calm, but there was some sporadic fire. Shells would fall sporadically. It was calm, the situation was calm, until sometime in the fall, October, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we save this map as it is marked. I don't believe that I will be revisiting it again as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell the Judges who was in the unit where you fought during the entire war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean who was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, who comprised the unit? Who were the people who were there with you in those positions, those locations where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, these were all people from the area, locals, who lived in this area, who were born in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you take up arms and why did you do so and who did -- who issued you with the rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I got my rifle from the Territorial Defence, and then the Territorial Defence became the Republika Srpska Army after the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know just a brigade commander, Miodrag Sejhovac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you tell us that it was quiet all the way up to October. And what happened then, in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in 1994 I was in Vojkovici as a member of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, because it covered that area in the direction of Kijevo and Trnovo. I spent most of my time there, and then we were sent further south from Vojkovici from time to time. That did -- had not happened in the previous period, but it did in that period because we sustained some heavy attacks from the Muslim -- by the Muslim forces from Igman, Bjelasnica, and Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me, when was the last offensive launched by the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the last offensive launched by the Republika Srpska army in the area where I was, in the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, was in 1993. That was Operation Lukavac. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how did it end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it ended -- in fact, my brigade went all the way up to the summit of Igman without encountering any resistance. We didn't fight because they had already pulled out, and then we had to wait a couple of days there because there was some negotiations mediated by the international community with our leadership. And then after that, we had to pull out to our starting positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were talking about October and November 1994. These were the offensives that were launched by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1994, the Muslims launched the offensives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you were there in the Trnovo area. What was going on in the Trnovo area? Were there any clashes there and who suffered casualties in those clashes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1994, the Serbian army and the Serbian people suffered casualties in the clashes there, I mean the local Serbian population, because our troops sustained a fierce offensive, fierce attacks, infantry attacks, artillery attacks on our positions and we were able to hold it off for some 15 days. And then when I was rotated and when I went back to our positions at Vojkovici and some other people manned this position, the line was broken through and the enemy came all the way up to Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what the people wanted to do in those moments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was chaos in Trnovo for the civilians. General Milosevic went there to try to calm the people down; that's what I learned from the people there when I came back. And people in Trnovo were thankful to him for that, and he gave them his support. He told them that they should remain there in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did those offensives peter out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did this lull -- for how long did this lull last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now I'm talking about the area covered by the 2nd Brigade. There were some sporadic shellings of the civilians and some machine-gun fire was opened on Vojkovici and Sarajevo-Trnovo road, but the lull lasted until sometime in August, August, September, October of the next year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you said that there was a lull. Could you please define when it began and when it ended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the beginning of 1995, all the way up to August of that year, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that sanctions were imposed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the war ended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in 1995, in the fall, after the Dayton Peace Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what happened in June and July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In June and July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1995. Yes, yes. I think that a lot of troops, their troops, left Sarajevo to go to Mount Igman, and they moved across the mountain in the direction of our brigade and they moved further up north to other axes. It could be observed as they climbed up Mount Igman and as they left Butmir, Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So were you able to see that from the place you were? And how were they leaving? What route did they take as they moved towards those axes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was able to see that from my home. When I went there to bring some humanitarian aid, supplies, to my relatives or to do some work in the garden, I was able to see them move out of the tunnel and I was able to observe the entire route moving -- leading to Mount Igman. They had done so before in 1994. But on the other side, as they climbed down Mount Igman, we were also able to see that there were columns and columns, military columns, fighting vehicles, and infantry, a large number of troops leaving -- getting out of the tunnel. We could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any casualties, military or civilian, that summer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's at the very end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that because in August, in late August, my father-in-law was seriously wounded - my wife told me that when I got home - in a church in Blazuj, at Ilidza. That was during a wedding. Muslim forces fired several shells that hit the church. All the wedding guests were wounded. He was seriously wounded, and some other people were also seriously wounded, but I know for sure about my father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, this was an incident that was not disclosed in any regard in the 65 ter summary for this witness, and I will be, of course, cross-examining him on that. I may try or seek to cross-examine him with some additional documentation as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't get any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is that? I can tell you what Ms. Edgerton said. Well, I'll ask Ms. Edgerton to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to indicate that this was not an incident which was disclosed in any regard in the 65 ter summary for this witness. I'm not mounting an objection, but I'm going to -- I'm indicating right now I'm going to be cross-examining him on that, and I may seek to cross-examine him with some additional documentation to that which was disclosed at the beginning of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I simply would like to know if the witness could tell us in the area where he lived in this period that he was mostly talking about, so in this area where he lived, in the areas where he participated in those conflicts, if he could tell us how many civilians were killed or wounded and how many of his fellow fighters, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, that's simply not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, if this is not relevant and if it is not relevant that so many lives were lost in the combat activities, even on this side, and that this side faced a necessity, in particular in a period when it did not launch any offensives anymore, then if we are to accept what my learned colleague from the Prosecution has said, then the Defence should rest its case right now and not deal with any issues. If this is not relevant - and I'm not talking about the tu quoque principle; I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- combat activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you talking about? Show us how it is relevant to an issue in the indictment. Because I'm inclined to agree with the Prosecutor, and I'll consult my colleagues, unless you can persuade me otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We wrote a motion today discussing all those issues, and I believe that this motion that was submitted regarding the request not to call the next witness, I think that we addressed this very issue in that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the main reason why I disallowed the Prosecutor's motion was that in paragraph 7 of your response you said the witness would be speaking about the geographical location of the hospital surrounded by hills controlled by the ABiH. That's an issue in this case, who controlled the hills. I have no interest, the Chamber has absolutely no interest, in the number of Serbs that were killed, unless it relates to a specific issue, no matter how hurtful that may be to you or to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have told you before that I am not conducting an historical or sociological survey into the Sarajevo conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm asking for 30 seconds to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours did not mention paragraph 14 of our submission in connection with the motion to exclude a witness, but all the victims in this conflict show that the VRS was not facing civilians as a population and nothing more, but there were two warring sides, and it was not that civilians predominated on one side, and that's what we explained in your submission. All the victims, I will to God that there had been none on either side, but it all shows that it was not civilians opposing the VRS, as the indictment claims. And that's the major issue here, because according to the allegations in the indictment, it was always civilians facing the Army of Republika Srpska, but it was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact, that had civilians on both sides under its control. And it was not civilians who were facing the VRS but another army. All the civilian victims on either side, and I regret that there were any civilian victims on either side, are a result of the fact that there were two armies facing one another. The indictment alleges that civilians were being fired on as if there were no two opposing armies. Therefore, the casualties on both sides show precisely this, and the Army of Republika Srpska was not facing civilians. Had that been the case, this would be the most horrendous crime in the history of civilisation, if that were so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you have anything to say in reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. Let me consult with Mr. Waespi for a moment on this one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, so are you saying, then, that you will be bringing evidence through this witness that the victims in this part of the conflict were not civilians but -- but what? This is what I'm not clear about. What will you be saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not drawing a distinction between civilians and soldiers. What I'm saying is that there were victims on both sides who were both civilians and soldiers. I'm just trying to submit that the Army of Republika Srpska did not have before it civilians, but instead it had before it a strong, well-armed army, especially in the time-period relative to the indictment. And some foreign observers even said that this other army was stronger than the VRS. Therefore, the VRS was not targeting civilians at any point, but it was doing what is usually done in armed conflicts. And I can go into this further when the time comes. However, the indictment is representing the case as if the VRS had before it civilians and was firing on civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't understand the Prosecution to be saying that at some time the VRS did not fight with the ABiH army; I understand them to be saying that at some time the VRS specifically targeted civilians and that was done as part of the war strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is but one segment of the indictment. We will challenge each one of those incidents. In our view, not a single one of those incidents which are supposed to be representative of the actions of the VRS has been proved beyond reasonable doubt. The entire indictment rests on the case that everything the VRS did was done against civilian facilities and civilians. Nowhere in the counts in the indictment and the paragraphs of the indictment is it mentioned that this was an armed conflict between two armies on those locations. I could do again what I did the other day. Every time it says "the civilian population of Sarajevo," the civilian population of Sarajevo; however, the civilian population of Sarajevo is a very broad concept, this includes Grbavica, this includes Nedzarici, this includes Ilidza, the civilian population of Sarajevo also includes Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What troubles me in all this, Your Honour, is that I can't seem to get away, because I see this theme repeated, from what appears to be an assertion by Mr. Tapuskovic that, if I understand him correctly, that the victims in this conflict were not civilians. I've just heard him say something to this effect again, Your Honours. And if that's one of the defences that Mr. Tapuskovic is going to put forward on behalf of his client, it's something that should have been put to the witnesses as part of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe so, but that doesn't prevent him from putting it now. In an ideal case, yes, in an ideal situation, yes, I agree, it should have been put forward as part of the defence through cross-examination, but I don't believe that precludes him from putting it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, the problem the Trial Chamber faces is to understand what your defence strategy is, because we have an indictment, we have an accused, and we need to understand what you are saying to see whether he is proved responsible or not. This is what we are currently doing at the moment. So in this case, you have mentioned the incident that has been explained by the witness. This is in 1995, this happened in his village, and he tells a story and he tells us how the -- the representatives of his community who were attending a wedding were hit by shells in the church and a lot of the guests were injured in the process. This piece of evidence which you are adducing, what are you trying to prove thereby? Does this mean that among the Serb population there were people who were injured and that there were casualties, and on the other hand, there are also people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Muslims who were also -- faced the same plight who were injured? Are you saying, in other words, that there was collateral damage on both sides and this was due to the fighting between the two armies? So by telling us that there were Serb victims, you are challenging the submission of the Prosecution; in other words, the Army of Republika Srpska was deliberating targeting the civilian population. Is that what you're saying? Let me resume. It is because the ABiH army caused collateral damage on the Serb side that the victims -- part of the ABiH army can't have been deliberately targeted by the Republika Srpska. Is that what you are trying to prove?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honour, Judge Mindua, you have just defined what is at issue here. Why victims of the Serb side among civilians and soldiers and why the casualties on the Bosniak side among civilians and soldiers. And we come to the time-period concerning the accused, Milosevic. What I'm saying is that that was a time when there were quite a few lulls in the fighting and at that time the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was far stronger than the Army of Republika Srpska, so the Army of Republika Srpska was unable to carry out any operations or activities. I'm not dealing with history here, and if need be, I can drop the historian I was intending to call. What we have to look at are the circumstances that existed in the relevant time-period. Why would there be victims on the Serb side if this was not an armed conflict. The Prosecution case which one can see running through the indictment from the first count onwards, that they were shelling the civilian population of Sarajevo. So this case that the civilian population were the targets does not hold water, and this is the main case in the indictment. One cannot have victims on only one side. Why would there be victims on the other side if there was no conflict? We are challenging, we are absolutely challenging. You mentioned collateral damage. We will certainly be dealing with that here, and it's certainly something that can be discussed here. But that the only aim and intention of the Army of the Republika Srpska was to fire on civilians is something I absolutely exclude. The Defence has many documents and witnesses to show the reverse, that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was, in fact, targeting civilians. But in fact, we can only speak of collateral damage in this two-sided conflict, because the casualties on the Serb side, both military and civilian, are not unconnected to everything that was going on. There might have been people retaliating for something they themselves experienced personally. But to put the case that the Army of Republika Srpska was facing only civilians and targeting civilians and civilian facilities only, if this was its only goal, if that would be proved, then the judgement against General Galic and any judgement that might be passed against General Milosevic would show that this was one of the most horrendous crimes ever committed. I would like to add, Your Honours, by your leave, that in my country at present -- may I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we have heard enough. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I would just like to make one brief point because it almost turned into a closing argument. What the Defence consistently disregards are that even during what the Defence says are lulls and I think the witness said March to October 1994 and January to June 1994 [sic], although the witness sort of talked about August 1995, we have numerous incidents of attacks on civilians inside the confrontation lines. We have sniping incidents. We have attacks by air-bombs during these periods the Defence calls lulls. So even during that period -- or during that period, there is certainly no issue of collateral damage and the Defence just disregards that, or these other incidents of indiscriminate shelling into civilian areas, the Defence brushes it aside. Just look at the indictment, look at the incidents, the shelled incidents, we even dropped the third, Your Honour. These are illustrative examples of sniping of civilians inside the confrontation line and that's the issue and that's, I suggest, what the Defence should be opposing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber disallows the question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, for your recollection I could read out the question to you again. You asked the witness if he could tell how many civilians were killed or wounded and how many of his fellow fighters, soldiers. That was the question and we have disallowed it, and we kindly ask you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question that has been disallowed, should I understand that to mean that I cannot ask anyone anymore about what happened to people from the other side in these activities and the combat if that is the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Carry on. Each case will be determined on its own merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I'm going to wait, but then I'm in a dilemma because of that situation. Perhaps the Defence will have to do something over the next few days in some sense. Perhaps we will decide then to ask for time to prepare to submit our closing statement. I don't know if we're going to be able to do that, because we believe that in circumstances like these the Defence has been prevented from justly conducting its case, and it can happen that very soon we can ask to maybe hear an expert, perhaps not even an expert, and then to thank you, and then to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- move towards closing the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you have heard the Chamber's ruling. Move on to your next question. I don't want to hear arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm going to have to take my arguments quickly. I thank the witness very much. I have no other questions. And I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me and understand me in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have too many questions of you and we'll probably take a break before I'm concluded, but perhaps we can begin with something rather general. Mr. Witness, you've never met the accused in this case, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never met him, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've never met any senior staff whatsoever of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're not then aware -- you have no personal knowledge of any orders that they might have issued regarding the shelling of Bosnian-held areas of Sarajevo, the sniping of those areas, or the use of air-bombs against those parts of Sarajevo that were held by Bosnian forces, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is too long. I didn't understand it, but I think that it's like this. I don't know. I never had the opportunity to receive or to have access to any documents. I wasn't at that level, to be able to see something like that during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: During the course of the conflict, from April 1992 until November 1995, you were an ordinary soldier, weren't you, a soldier in the trenches, if we can call it like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On Bosnian Serb-held territory. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: During the course of the conflict, you never had occasion to travel into any parts of the city of Sarajevo that were held by Bosnian forces, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never did go.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Never having been inside that territory, you were never in a position to see or personally experience the bombardment of that territory, the sniping of that territory, the privation suffered by anybody, civilians in particular who lived inside those lines, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't go and I couldn't experience the suffering of those people, and I regret their suffering. But I also went through my own suffering in my own way that -- at the hands of their army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand you have views on that, and you can be certain that I sympathise with those. But I wanted to ask you: You've, before you're testifying today, not had an opportunity to look at the indictment against the accused in this case, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you don't then know that he stands charged with crimes against the civilian population inside that part of Sarajevo that was held by Bosnian forces, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the only thing you can tell us today is of what you saw or heard from other people about what happened outside those confrontation lines, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question I believe should not be permitted, if he found out and in what way he found out. I think that we need to remain within the limits of what this witness can say. I think that the way it was framed by my learned friend is something that is not permissible. But I'll leave it up to Your Honours to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand why you say it's not permissible. She's merely trying to find out the source of the information that he's giving us today. How did he acquire that information? Did he hear it from anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was outside of the bounds, so it was outside the confrontation lines. The witness said that he didn't understand, but I didn't understand either. Which confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was: "The only thing you can tell us today is of what you saw or heard from other people about what happened outside those confrontation lines?" What's the answer to that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the war -- I cannot answer that because some things I saw, some things I heard, some things I don't know about. They were maybe passed on by someone else. You hear information from someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question before the break or --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps a good moment to take the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- because I would show an exhibit after this, and we can set that up during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to be very brief with you now. Just a couple of questions based on what you've said earlier today. You talked in your testimony on -- about page 16 about columns and columns of troops and vehicles, military vehicles, and infantry coming out of the tunnel. And what I'd like to know about that -- in fact, let me ask you. You couldn't actually see the exit from the tunnel, could you? You couldn't actually see the vehicles coming out of the tunnel, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think probably one last question then. How far -- or are you in a position to estimate approximately how far from the Sarajevo city centre, let's say Marin Dvor area, how far it is from there to Trnovo as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trnovo is 24 kilometres away, so from the bus and the train station in Sarajevo to Trnovo, it's about 24 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Those are all the questions I have for you, Mr. Witness. And thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would you please permit me a direct question? If not, you can deny me the right to put that question. I would like to ask the witness if he had ever heard about the order to find a civilian and deprive him of or fire at him. Did he ever hear of an order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean by "direct," that it doesn't arise from the cross-examination? If we allow it, then the Prosecutor will be allowed, of course, to ask another question. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that I have never heard of such an order from anyone or anywhere during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And -- well, had somebody said something to that effect to you - and this is my last question - what would you have said or done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an idiot to obey something like that, do something like that, I can think with my own head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness -- well, I want to find out whether the Prosecutor wishes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: She does not wish to ask any questions. So Witness T-39, that concludes your evidence. We are grateful to you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness will be Witness T-42, Dr. Milan Pejic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No protective measures have been sought, so we don't need the blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you please tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were born on the 13th of June, 1948?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, in Blazuj, in the Blazuj neighbourhood, in the section of the city called Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You finished elementary school in Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You finished the gymnasium in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the medical faculty in Sarajevo in 198 -- in 1974?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You specialised in the diseases of the ear, throat, and nose, in the Kosevo clinic in 1983?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the hospital in Kosevo, you worked until -- from 1979?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the events in question began in Sarajevo in 1992, you were the director of the clinic, the ENT clinic, at Kosevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, the ear, nose, and throat clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 8th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, but on the 8th of May, 1992, was the last time that I was at the clinic. I was discharged of my duties as director of the clinic a little bit later, and I wasn't informed about it directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's not go into all of that, and I'm just asking you, before the 8th of May were there any problems with some people who were wounded somewhere; and if so, what happened in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to renew the objections I made with the previous witness. Wounded people before the 8th of May, 1992, in my submission isn't relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, how do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until yesterday the Prosecution was putting questions to the witnesses from 1992 onwards, and the indictment includes the time-period when we're talking about general circumstances from 1992, that's what it states in each count of the indictment. And now all of a sudden -- I would be very grateful if we were just to deal with the time-frame of the indictment, but the indictment every day speaks of the time-period from the 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't mean that any and everything that happened from 1992 is relevant, you know. Your task is to show us how the evidence about the wounded people that you are seeking to elicit from this witness is relevant to the indictment. Is it relevant to any paragraph in the indictment? Is there any paragraph in the indictment that addresses this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So far at least it is possible and so far at least we talked about -- well, paragraph 29, I don't have it in front of me, that it was not disputed that there was an armed conflict in the area of Yugoslavia as well as the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Does that mean now that we cannot talk about at all about things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you want to tell us why do you want this evidence? Why do you want this evidence of the wounded people? You must want it for a purpose. What is your reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he's going to tell you that it was not possible to help those people; and for that reason, they died and they were wounded. Why wasn't it possible to give them assistance? We can explain. In relation to these two people and what prompted him to continue to act as a doctor who had given the Hippocratic oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's precisely the problem. How is this anything more than evidence of Serb suffering. Evidence of Serb suffering is not, per se, relevant. You must be able to link it to some issue in the indictment because the indictment is about ABiH -- principally about ABiH civilians who were targeted. So merely for you in response to provide evidence of Serb suffering doesn't answer the charges. And what's more, it may be said not to be relevant, and that's the problem you are facing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are other matters which on the basis of the response that you gave to the Prosecutor's motion to exclude the evidence of this witness, which are -- are very relevant. The -- identified the -- what I call paragraph 7, the -- that he would testify on all aspects of the Zica Hospital's daily running, of which he was a director; in particular on the military status of patients; the geographical location of the hospital surrounded by hills controlled by the ABiH. That's what is relevant: The geographical location of the hospital and that it was surrounded by hills allegedly controlled by the ABiH. That's the most important aspect of the -- of this witness's evidence. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just a general point. We have the situation before with a witness I think of Mr. Sachdeva. When we are talking about what the witness is going to say and the importance or the relevancy for Your Honours, I think it would be prudent to have the witness removed, especially if it's a lengthy discussion. It's also, I think, not fair to expose the witness to these procedural witnesses. I just saw that Mr. Tapuskovic said the witness is going to say about this, this, this. I'm not saying the witness is couching his answers to that, but if we anticipate lengthy discussions about what the witness is going to say and the relevance of it, I think as its been done in other Trial Chambers, I think the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not following that procedure; I don't see any merit in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask you to also take note of paragraphs 13 and 14 of our submissions regarding this doctor, because we dealt with a question there that is quite important to us, us in the Defence, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- that he will testify about the geographical location of the hospital, you know, and the question of who controlled the surrounding hills. And the other one which follows, that he will testify about the entire population within a radius of several kilometres, still within the boundaries of the city of Sarajevo, going to that hospital for all kinds of medical care between 22nd of April, 1992, and the Dayton Accords. I don't myself immediately see its relevance. What would be the relevance of that? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last paragraph, paragraph 14, Your Honour, Judge Robinson, it's actually -- it finalizes everything, and evidently you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have a difficulty in understanding what you are trying to say in paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the interpreters to translate paragraph 14, because we had some difficulty understanding it, and it may have arisen from a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a very serious matter, in my opinion, really important. When you quoted our -- our answer, our arguments, we were quite surprised that you left out, so to speak, the conclusion of our arguments. Because actually all of our argument is -- is organised according to what comes before and what comes after. You have to read the whole thing in the right sequence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I wasn't quite sure, but now I understand that you didn't get a translation in English of that particular paragraph, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have an official translation and it matters not that I did not mention it explicitly, because I did not say that this evidence will be allowed to give will be confined to any particular paragraph. In fact, I said explicitly at the very end that the whole purpose of the decision was to answer the Prosecution's motion which was to exclude his evidence. And that still left the Trial Chamber with its obligation to see that any evidence given is relevant. So it's perfectly open to Mr. Tapuskovic to seek to lead any evidence from any of the paragraphs mentioned in the response. In fact, even if it is not there, the Trial Chamber will decide in the usual way as to whether an issue of relevance arises and determine it. But I'm going to ask the interpreter to translate for us paragraph 14 of the Defence response, and for that purpose we should put it on the -- on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could somebody please read the text that needs to be translated and then it can be translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, would you read the text so that it can be translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. "Given that the number of patients cared for at the Zica Hospital in the time mentioned and that the nature of their wounds and the causes of their deceased show together with other evidence introduced by Defence that contrary to the indictment, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was not fighting the civilian population, as that population could not have been the origin of so many deaths and so many wounded people on the territory under its control. And the military activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were not aimed at the civilian population." Your Honour, I want to add one thing. The link introduced in this paragraph, since the paragraphs are to be read in sequence, so there is a legal reasoning behind it, and you will find that link in paragraph 11. That's where we speak of the relevant paragraph in the indictment, that paragraph with which the testimony and the facts on which the testimony rest are to be linked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the paragraph in the indictment that's referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all the counts, that's the counts from 1 to 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not very helpful, Ms. Isailovic. Counts 1 to 7, I would have thought you would be a little more specific. I'll ask -- I'm still not clear what the paragraph means. Would either Mr. Tapuskovic or Ms. Isailovic explain the purport of that paragraph which was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we really weighed every word in our motion, bearing in mind, in particular, the general allegations in the paragraphs of the indictment that pertain to Dragomir Milosevic. And if you were to quote from any paragraph, you would see that all the activities from paragraph, let's say, 5 only discuss the sniper and artillery campaign against the civilian population in Sarajevo. Where -- how come that there were so many civilian casualties on the other side? But leaving that aside, if you read any paragraph thereafter, in particular the counts of the indictment, they only talk about civilian targets. And there has been no evidence as yet that the Republika Srpska Army had as its sole goal to fire on civilian targets and people living in Sarajevo, and that this was the sole reason for guiding all of their activities. What we wanted to say is that because there were civilian casualties in other areas, we draw no distinction in Sarajevo between Grbavica and Stari Grad, between Nedzarici, Vrace, Ilidza, Hadzici, Hrasnica, we make no distinction. There were tragedies in all of those areas, and the Republika Srpska army -- never did the Republika Srpska army position itself against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I fail to understand the meaning of the sentence in paragraph 14 in which you say, and I'm quoting: [Interpretation] "Contrary to the counts on the -- in the indictment, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was not fighting the civilian population because that population could not have been the origin of so many wounded and fatalities on the territory that it controlled." [In English] Or are you saying here that victims were imported to the crime scenes or -- what is the meaning of this allegation or this sentence in your paragraph 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't say that here. That's not what it means. We wrote this text together in French and then it was interpreted by my colleague and I am sure that she is much better or no worse than I am in the niceties of the French language, but this is not what we are alleging. Of course we will be showing in some cases that this was done in some cases. But I cannot now deal with specific cases. As a matter of principle, no, this was just this thing that you said, but my colleague can explain those nuances and there were such events but this was not the general, widespread occurrence. We will be dealing that when the time comes. Perhaps my colleague could assist Judge Harhoff because of her ability with the French language and its nuances, if you allow her to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would allow her to do so. Please just tell us what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sorry that I wasn't able to listen to the English translation at the same time that I was reading it. I would probably have to look at the transcript of the English translation, but as I explained -- well, that may be sort of French formulation of things. The paragraph is a reasoning, and as I was saying there is a logical sequence of the paragraphs, the end of it being the conclusion of the argument. If you take everything that was explained before, what we're saying, what the Defence is saying here, is that the indictment is blaming the accused for having organised a campaign -- they're calling the acts of the accused by a campaign of sniping and shelling aimed at civilians, which is -- which is what the indictment does throughout. Basically, as my colleague was saying, it appears in every paragraph, and it culminates in the counts, 1 to 7, and that's what we're talking about throughout is this campaign of shelling and sniping against civilians. From this, we draw the qualification of war crimes and crimes against humanity. But actually, the facts on which this particular witness as well as other witnesses can make a statement if you ask them direct questions about the victims that -- that were on the territory controlled by the VRS, what you can ask these people to do is precisely to state, to establish the fact -- and it seems clear to me that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was not fighting civilians. Hence, because of the number of the victims, because of the type of wounds that they had, shells and -- mortar shells and bullets, et cetera, we can draw that conclusion and we ask the Chamber to draw the same conclusion, which is that these wounds are the results of military acts, that is, military fighting; that facing the ABiH, we don't have a simple population of civilian victims but an army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Isailovic. We've heard enough. We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we have to be very specific and we really have to deal with the key issues pertaining to your job and your experiences. I wanted to conduct this examination-in-chief in a different way, but guided as I am by the Trial Chamber, I will now move on to the specific question. What happened with the two wounded people? I don't know who they are, but what happened to them in that period, on the eve of the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I have to say that all my life, up until the Dayton Peace Agreements, I had lived in Blazuj, that's my home -- that's my home, and I travelled to the hospital in Kosevo. The last time that I was able to get to Kosevo was the 7th of May. After that, it was physically impossible to go to -- in Kosevo to go to work. If I had been able to go to work after that, I would have done so, but in early April, the Ministry of Health of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued a decree ordering all the health care workers to report to the first health care institution, the nearest health care institution, in case of an imminent threat of war or a state of emergency. Because there was an infirmary or a health care unit in Blazuj, I went there. I was actually called by a doctor and some nurses there, to treat those two wounded men and because of the way the building was constructed, we couldn't bring the two wounded men who were on the stretchers inside and we couldn't treat them. But unfortunately because of the nature of their injuries, they couldn't have been saved anyway. I think it was sometime in the 20th of April. I don't know if I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but what did you try to do but you were unable to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: We tried to bring them into the room where we could treat them. This was a GP clinic. You can take somebody's blood pressure, you can administer a shot, but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, your colleague just gave an explanation of paragraph 14 and some other paragraphs in your response, and that was what prompted me to answer -- to allow the question. She made a case for the question to be answered because part of the Defence case, as I understand it, is that wounds were suffered by people and those wounds were clearly inflicted by -- by military weaponry. I don't know what the Chamber will make of the case when we come to assess it at the end. I don't know what we will make of the argument, but that is the position that she presented. And as far as I'm concerned, it is on that basis that I allowed the question. That's the kind of evidence that you should be eliciting from this witness, not that he was prevented from carrying out his -- his functions. I don't see the relevance of that, and pretty soon Ms. Edgerton is going to be jumping up again, you know. And we don't want to put Ms. Edgerton to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I understand very well for your guidance and I thank you for it, but I wanted a doctor to show us the problems that they had been encountering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, at any rate, could you please tell the Judges what happened. I will no longer be cautioning you in any way, I will not be asking you questions, but could you please tell us what you were doing in the hospital throughout the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, you know quite well that there were two hospitals in Sarajevo, the general hospitals, the Kosevo and the former military hospital. In the area where I lived, there were no hospitals. As early as in April 1992, people felt very un -- unsafe, insecure about going to the hospital in Kosevo to -- for any treatment, for wounds or anything. In April, late April, an attack was carried out in Ilidza at a hotel in particular where there was an UNPROFOR base, and 35 people were killed -- were wounded and 14 people were killed in that attack. And it was impossible to treat those people in Sarajevo because people couldn't physically go there, and they didn't want to go to Sarajevo. And at that moment I, as a doctor, because I lived in that place, I treated the people in a motel, which was assigned by the Crisis Staff or the TO, I'm not sure what they were, for this purpose. I was able to give them just first aid to a very limited extent, and then those people were transported by various routes and means to Pale, so not to the military hospital, not to the Kosevo Hospital, but to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I would not want to qualify you as someone who is bent on having your own way, but it does seem like that, you know. What is the point of that evidence, the evidence which he has just given? I'm very sorry to hear, doctor, that you were not able to treat the wounded people in your own hospital, I'm sorry about that, but it doesn't help me in assessing this case. It has no bearing on this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I know that but how were those wounds inflicted? What caused these wounds? What happened? Let the doctor tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask him that. You're leading the evidence. Ask him that. This is your witness; control him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honours, but I feel so hemmed-in. I don't feel free to even ask him those simplest things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What caused these wounds and how -- how were these people wounded and how many of these wounded people there were in the four years of war, especially in the latter periods.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, while the hospital functioned in three years and ten months, we treated 5.800 people. I have the relevant records and I can place them at the disposal of anything who wants to check these allegations. A large number or large proportion of those wounded were civilians including children. I made an analysis for 1993, and in 1993 300 civilians were wounded, 61 children, and during our work in hospital, 440 people died of their wounds. I have to say that all those people who were wounded who received only minor injuries, never got to the hospital that I ran because there were health care centres in this area. Many of the wounded, especially at the beginning of the war, were shipped directly to Pale and Sokolac. So this is not the total. The number is higher, that's for sure. The wounds were caused by explosives, bullet-rounds, by sniper rounds. In the period while the hospital was in operation - I don't know whether this is relevant for the case or not - but in one period we treated patients that lived in an area controlled by the HVO, Kiseljak and Central Bosnia. I don't know whether this is enough for my answer. I could talk about it for days, but I don't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, do you have for each of these cases, for each of these persons, do you have records?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have records, definitely, for every person who entered the hospital, the protocol for all the patients who were hospitalised, we have a special protocol for all the patients who were -- who underwent surgery. And we actually submitted all those records to the Kasindol hospital, where I currently am employed as a director, and they are in the files there. Everybody can go there and check the records to see if they're accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were you able as a doctor - you told us that you are an ears, nose, and throat specialist - to notice what kind of wounds were predominant in the people who were brought there and on the basis of your immediate experience were you able to determine what caused the injuries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't see the cursor, so I don't know when I can start with my answer, but at any rate I have been a doctor for over 30 years. And at the time -- at the time when those unfortunate conflicts broke out, I had already accumulated quite a lot of experience, and I was able to determine the cause of the wounds. We also took X-rays of every wounded person, so it was possible to determine on the basis of the appearance of the wound and the examination of the patient what caused the wounds. Those were massive injuries caused by various kinds of explosives. We also had wounds caused by rounds fired from infantry weapons and during the lulls or cease-fires. Cease-fire agreements were signed at several times. We saw injuries caused by low-calibre weapons. We concluded that snipers had fired those shots because there had been no -- there had been no combat -- there was no combat at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you base your conclusions on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of X-rays, examinations, operative examinations, and also information that we obtained from those who actually brought the patients in, sometimes those were family members or whoever brought the patients in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who -- and where were those wounds caused, what part of the body?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
