utterances.text: Well, at times we were able to determine on the basis of the place where the injury was where actually this person was wounded. In some areas people were targeted in the head or in the pelvis or in the chest; in some areas, those people were more humane and they would target limbs. But we knew on the basis of where they had the wounds on their body we were able to determine the location from which they had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but I feel again I have to rise at this stage because my submission would be that this could be very relevant evidence if the people that the witness is discussing were killed or injured inside the confrontation lines. And without further detail or specification as to actually who these people were or where they came from, I question the relevancy of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, at that moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you to respond to the -- to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I didn't think that I was supposed to respond. I just thought that I should ask my question along those lines. But what this is all about is that the Defence is challenging this central location. What is inside the lines of confrontation? The witness might be able to shed some light on it. Who is holding the hills that dominate the area and that are very important in terms of the terrain relief around Sarajevo, and what was the situation in the area where his hospital was, what is going on there? Because it is the Defence's submission that the confrontation lines and what was inside the confrontation lines can be seen in various frameworks, the framework of Grbavica, of Nedzarici, of the old town, the framework of this area where the doctor worked. He can show you where his hospital was. He can tell you something about the geography of the area where the hospital was, and he could also talk about some of the positions of the Republika Srpska Army. And this is what I wanted to elicit in the course of my examination-in-chief. I wanted to ask him whether the hospital itself was targeted and from what direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to talk about the victims and more specifically those people who came to see you in your health centre. Where did these people come from? Were they coming from the area which was under the controlled -- under the control of the Republika Srpska or were they coming from the area under the control of the ABiH? What I mean, these people, your patients, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the area controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area where you were working, was it close to the confrontation line? From what I understood, you were quite far removed from the confrontation line according to what I understood from what Defence counsel has said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, can I indicate on the map where we were, and then you can gain an impression of the location of the hospital. The confrontation line --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a cut-out of a map available on e-court which shows great detail and that might assist the witness and everyone in answering Judge Mindua's question. I can offer even two options in terms of a 65 ter number, 02 -- pardon me. 02617A or 02617C, probably 2617C might be the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, we appreciate what you have tried to do, but the Prosecutor has offered on e-court a map so that you can look at it and just tell us what it is that you want to say. It's before you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hospital was located precisely where I am indicating, in this area here, in that -- no, it was here. I must explain that from the 22nd of April to early November, the hospital was in a motel in this building where I put the cursor now. But as it was quite clear that the war was not about to end, we had to look for another more suitable location for the winter. And we asked the municipality, which gave us a building which had previously been allotted to a company maintaining roads in Sarajevo. And this was on the Sarajevo-Mostar road. It was about 6 kilometres away from Nedzarici as the crow flies, and if you look towards Igman above Vrutak, it was about 5 kilometres or less. The Zica Hospital was located right here. It covered the area, or rather, its catchment area included five municipalities in the broader area of Sarajevo, and according to the information I then had there were about 90.000 people living in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Mindua was concerned to ascertain the distance between the hospital and the confrontation line, but the confrontation line isn't displayed on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's at the bottom right-hand corner, Your Honours, part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness indicate on this map so that Your Honours may understand -- I will switch on this other microphone. Could the witness approach and show where the hospital is and what there is around it and where the separation lines are and where the geographic areas are that overlooked the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it appears that that may offer a more graphic illustration. Please go ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hospital was in this location here, and you can see here that the catchment area of the hospital was on the front line, and the hospital was more or less surrounded. Before the airport was handed to UNPROFOR, we could get out via the airport; after that, we could get out through this line here, and we had to go around this whole part of Sarajevo. The wounded whom we assisted once we were equipped to provide assistance at a higher level had to travel to Pale or to Sokolac for five hours. Sokolac is somewhere here. They travelled for five hours. And in those transports there were others, civilians and soldiers, who were wounded additionally. You can imagine what it meant at that time to drive in military vehicles along macadam roads or dirt roads. The hospital I was in charge of had 80 beds, and every day I assert we had an average of ten wounded a day. Therefore, we always had to have sufficient beds free in order to receive and help the wounded who would be arriving. Our location was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These geographical positions, where were some of those characteristic hills in relation to your hospital? Can you show us that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: It's hard for me to see that. Igman was behind our backs. Excuse me. I think Igman is here. This part towards Hrasnica -- well, it's hard for me to find my way on this map. I'm no soldier, but I know that the elevations towards Sarajevo, such as Mojmilo, for example, was under BH army control, so was Zuc. I think these locations are somewhere here, Mojmilo and Zuc. Igman was on this side, if I'm correct. I don't know what other location there was. The hill of Stup, that was right here. All these other elevations were far away from us. The only high elevation in this area was this part of Igman. I think it's this part here. I apologise once again for not finding my way so easily on this map, but it was right above the hospital overlooking the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- objection that was made by Ms. Edgerton, and we have gone so far that I need to be reminded what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Mindua wanted to have some information before the Chamber ruled on that objection. I think it had to do with the evidence about wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. At page 48, line 14, the Prosecution's position was that the evidence with respect to the wounded was -- killed and wounded was only relevant to these proceedings where the indictment is exclusively concerned with people killed and wounded in Bosnian-held territory; that is, inside the confrontation lines. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In light of the explanation that has been given, the Chamber allows the question. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, perhaps you'll now find out from the witness about the hills and who held those hills and during what period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've already mentioned Stup, Zuc, Hum, Mojmilo, Igman behind your back. Who was holding all these positions? Can you explain that to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, although I'm a doctor and not a soldier, the positions you listed were held by the forces of the Bosnian Muslims or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were you doing, what were you focused on at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a doctor. I was treating people, helping the wounded and the sick, not just I, excuse me, it wasn't just me. I don't want it to appear that I was the only person working in that hospital. That hospital had 26 doctors working in it, 160 people working in that hospital. This was a general hospital. It had a maternity ward, incubators for babies. It was treating the entire population, the population surrounded by the front line on both sides with only a narrow passage out. There was no other protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this area where your hospital was, did you know something about the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska? For example, did you know the number of soldiers who were there, at least approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you a precise answer. I don't have this information, but I assume there could have been 5 or 6.000 soldiers, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many wounded did you say, 5.000 --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: 5.800 came to that hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say something about whether even in the most difficult times you could sometimes cross the airport with the sick or the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could, but I have to admit that it was a very torturous procedure. We had to explain quite clearly why the case was urgent. Each one of those sick or wounded was additionally checked by airport doctors working for the unit. I think it was the French Battalion, actually. So this happened very rarely with very difficult and torturous procedures and explanations as to why they had to go that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the patients who had to go the long way around, in addition to being wounded again, did they have other problems because they arrived at their destination late?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the problem -- what's the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if they could have gone across the airport, they might have been saved because it was an issue of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is the relevance of that if they could have been saved?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a humanitarian issue, but tell me how it relates to the issues in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's relevant because there is talk about blockades, encirclement, the difficulty of movement, and this shows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, move on to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems with medicines and how did you come by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tapuskovic, you don't seem to be comprehending what I've been saying. We are not interested in a general history of the problem. The evidence must relate to a particular issue in the indictment. So whether there are problems with medicines, I cannot see the relevance of that. Please move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case I will put a few questions such as the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were things easier when there was a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Certainly, because we would not have large numbers of wounded, but we still had very serious injuries caused by snipers. People were wounded individually, their injuries were very serious, and as I have said, we could tell by the part of the body that was injured - and now I'm referring to both soldiers and civilians indiscriminately - but by the part of the body that was injured, we could tell where they were coming from. It was very, very hard because there were children who were wounded in front of the school, while riding bicycles, in the streets. There was civilians who were wounded, women, children. I have information about this in the case histories, the protocols. You didn't tell me to prepare this and I won't go into it, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you can substantiate everything you say with the appropriate documentation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please also tell the Judges a little bit about the time in between, for example, the period from the end of May until the end of the war, was there anything out of the ordinary that was going on? I'm talking about 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995 there were intense attacks, especially in the area covered by the hospital by the forces of the B&H army. There was a well-known offensive in which we had a large number of wounded. It was just shelling, indiscriminate shelling, and other than this I would like to note just one incident that I directly witnessed from the windows of the hospital. It happened on the 28th of August, 1995, in front of the church that was 500 metres away from the hospital. And I watched as shells fell, they were getting closer and closer and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry again, but this has become a recurring theme. The suffering of the people who lived in Bosnian Serb-occupied territory is absolutely regrettable and very tragic, but it's not what is on trial here, Your Honours. So I would object to the relevance of this unless it goes directly to the -- one of the issues closest to the responsibility of the accused in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] My microphone was not activated. Does it go to any of the issues, this evidence which we are about to hear; if not, we'll just move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This specific example that the witness cited can have a certain meaning - I'm not insisting on it, though - but the entire question and all the things that we talked about now is connected to our debate a little bit earlier, and you allowed the witness to speak about things that do have direct links with the combat actions that caused these consequences among the civilians and soldiers. So my question had to do with the key indictment period relating to events between May and the end of the war, and the witness said that at that time there were many civilian casualties. I can go on to ask him if the hospital was sometimes directly hit also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Please wait for my ruling. Yes, go ahead and ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was the hospital ever directly shelled from any military positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Shells fell around the hospital, quite close to the hospital, on several occasions, and there was a direct hit immediately next to the hospital on the 6th or the 8th of September, 1995, when some of our patients were killed and when some of the hospital staff were wounded. I don't know who fired, but at the time I assume that these would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Ms. Edgerton is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I should note that the shelling of the hospital was not in the 65 ter summary nor was it contained in any of the pleadings we received this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It doesn't appear to me, Mr. Tapuskovic, that you have much more to get from this witness on that issue. So move on to another -- another topic, and please remember that you're well past the time allotted for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I actually just wanted to -- and I wanted to finish with that so that's when the intervention of the Prosecutor came. But that offensive that we were talking about, how many patients came to you in that period, primarily civilians, but then all others seeking medical help and what sort of injuries or wounds were involved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I really cannot give a proper answer to your question, because I did not prepare for such a question. But it's certain that there were a large number of wounded, but I cannot be precise about the number because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what kinds of wounds were involved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: These were quite significant wounds, various types of explosive wounds using infantry and other types of weapons or ammunition. They were very destructive injuries, and we invested a lot of effort to save the lives of these people. There was a large number of civilians wounded that were wounded along with soldiers, but I really don't know the number at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you were to look at the documentation, would you be able to provide us with a precise number?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I can begin, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Pejic, you've said several times in answering questions from Mr. Tapuskovic that you're not a soldier. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't hear a translation of his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wasn't a soldier. I'm not a military person, I'm a civilian, from the civilian sector, from the Kosevo Hospital. But during the war all people of my age received a war assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: The hospital, just let me say this. My hospital was a general hospital where people worked according to a decision by the Secretariat by the Secretariat for National Defence. I received a work duty assignment, I don't know what it's called. But I worked at the hospital without wearing a military uniform, if you understand me. Some staff in that hospital was by establishment, part of the 4th Medical Battalion, but this was less than 50 per cent of the total medical staff which employed 160 people. They went through a kind of accelerated training, that's what it's called. So about 70 people of different profiles consisted of this 2nd Company of the 4th Medical Battalion that worked at the hospital, the general hospital. We operated as a general hospital directly under the control of the Ministry for Defence of Republika Srpska, but we were not necessarily mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, and you touched on that in your evidence in chief, so I did understand that you were mobilised in your capacity as a medical health professional and you did report for duty in the hospital which you later came to work in. But to go back to my original question, not being a soldier, then you would have no personal knowledge, I take it, of any orders issued by the accused regarding the use of ammunition, shells, bullets, air-bombs, or any action against targets within Bosnian-controlled territory in the city of Sarajevo, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I didn't have any access or control over that, but I didn't have any control over those who fired at us. You must understand that we were also fired at. I was the eye-witness of two massacres of civilians at the bus station in Ilidza on the 26th -- please let me answer, if you permit me. This is very important. On the 26th of October, 1992, I was directly at the location when the bus stop -- the bus station was hit and when 35 civilians were wounded and eight were killed. The second incident was at a church, it was a wedding of a person, and these were civilians, and you could see it very well from the --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Pejic, you've been in this courtroom when you heard all the parties have long discussions about what is the evidence that is most germane and relevant to the case that we're trying here today. So if you would just let me -- while I understand these are very important to you, let me guide you with my questions and your answers, I would really appreciate that. Thank you. During the course of the conflict, I take it from your testimony in chief you never had occasion to travel into -- no, let me rephrase the question, if I may. What knowledge do you have, Dr. Pejic, about the sniping or shelling of civilians in Sarajevo and the injuries they sustained as a result over the course of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Just indirectly, not directly, because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that indirect knowledge, how did you gain that? Was it through the media? Was it what people told you or was it from what you read or all of those sources?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Through the media, by television, because Television Sarajevo quite frequently broadcast segments from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you are aware and prepared to concede that there was shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo throughout 1992, right through to 1995, throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I really wouldn't be able to comment on your question, but in any case that did happen. As for what happened, how it happened, well first of all I was primarily busy by providing medical treatment to the people that needed it, so I didn't really follow the political or the other developments so much, but I did see something that related to that on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion at any time over the course of the conflict to your recollection to treat civilians who had been injured as a result of shelling or sniping within Bosnian-held territory, from within the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: How could I have been there when I was on this side? That was simply impossible. People, wounded people, on both sides would go to their own hospitals. Only if somebody of the citizens living in the area that was covered by my hospital but was not of Serb ethnicity, they would come for treatment to the hospital where I worked, where we were providing medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Out of the number of patients then that you would have treated of non-Serb ethnicity, Bosnian first, what proportion of the patients would they represent, what number?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I think that there were very few, very few, but in any case it's something that could be counted if we looked at the records. All the people who could come to the hospital were received equally, they received equal treatment, and they would be discharged in the same way that people who were ethnic Serbs were discharged. There was some Muslims and there were also some Croats who had come to the hospital for treatment, so you could even ask them. I could give you the names of those people about the kind of treatment. I mean, I wouldn't be able to provide these names to you today, but I could do it a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honours, would it be time to take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Pejic, I only have a few more brief questions for you, if I may. During your testimony in chief you gave evidence saying positions at Stup, Zuc, Hum, and Mojmilo hill were to your knowledge held by Bosnian forces. Could I just ask you, is the basis of your knowledge for this similar to your knowledge of sniping and shelling of Sarajevo in that you learned it from the media and you heard about it or read about it from other people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, I simply knew that because it was very close to the hospital where I worked, and I knew where the lines were, where the front lines were. And they were not manned by Serbs, and there was no need for me to find that out indirectly through the media, I lived there. I was able to see those hills. There is a line of sight to those hills from the hospital, and it would be, in fact, good if we could actually go to this building and then you will be able to see what you can see. We were in a valley, or rather, in a flat area that was dominated by those hills. Those hills dominated the place where our hospital was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you've never been to the front lines, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely. I never went there, but it's just a couple of kilometres away as the crow flies, and you were able to see where the fighting was going on at the confrontation lines there you can see -- you could see where the wounded were coming in from. And in 1992 and the beginning of 1993, Serbs who lived at Zuc hill came to the hospital. The wounded, those who were killed, to the hospital where I worked. The attack had been launched from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. Given your answers about what you've said about the front lines, I wonder if I could have a map put on your screen bearing the 65 ter number 02617A. Do you see the map on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a map here, but I don't know the number. I think it's 05 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You do see a map in front of did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: -- 0984 -- yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, this represents, if I can say, it's not as magnified a version, a wider view of the same map you looked at earlier. I wonder if you can look at the map and identify similarly to what you did before, your hospital or the approximate location, which should stand pretty much in the centre of what you see in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would be quite glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- could you please mark that and perhaps mark a letter "B" for the word hospital in your language, "bolnica"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I will put a cross and the word "H," that's the usual symbol for a hospital -- well, that will be it here. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Now, sir, would you agree with me that this map represents the area in and around your hospital and a pretty accurate, since you've seen them, representation of the confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume so. I didn't mark them myself, but I assume that -- yes, that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on what you've said you've been able to see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then perhaps just one last question, if you can go south of the location you've marked as your hospital, immediately before the number 4 there's a location depicted there with the name Lokve on it. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see the designation of the high point just a little bit further south of Lokve as 1246, 1246 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: No, I can't see it. I can see where it says Lokva, not Lokve with an "E." Lokva is another place name in another place --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: So this is, in fact, one of the summits there at Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you look at the base of the little flag immediately before Lokva, the designation 1246 marking the height of the elevation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. That's a rather steep elevation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Which one do you mean, do you mean the 1246? Yes, yes. Well, in fact, the whole mountain is quite steep. This part of Mount Igman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could he just mark this elevation for me that you're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think he could, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you do that, Dr. Pejic, mark the elevation at the summit of Lokva.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Lokva or 1246? This here is Lokva.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 1246, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: That's the elevation here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you put the number 1 beside the elevation that you've just marked, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can see it. I hope I got that right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me, doctor, that that elevation is somewhat steeper than Zuc, which is approximately 850 metres; Mojmilo, which is about 500 metres; Hum, also about 500 metres, those locations that you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand, what do you mean when you say "steep"? If you say "steep," that refers to the gradient, but if you want to say that it's high, yes, in that case it is higher, indeed, because 1.246 metres, that is, indeed higher than, let's say, 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if I could have this map marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You accept the correction? You're speaking of height, not of steepness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P780, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions for the doctor, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just regarding this map, which is still in front of us, that's Exhibit P780.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the part of Mount Igman, which as you indicated was inside this line here. Now, to the east of this elevation that you marked, where does Mount Igman extend to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: To the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To the south?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What elevations are there in that area in relation to those elevations that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know their height, but I do think that there are some that are higher than this summit. Although I was actually born at the foothills of Igman, I don't know about that. But perhaps we could look at the map and then we will be able to ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or perhaps some other map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we perhaps scroll down this map -- no, Your Honour, I don't have a map here, but Igman extend -- extends --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have 02617, the complete map, available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's have it then displayed. In the meantime, Doctor, were you able to see from the hospital the -- the -- who occupied the top of those hills, Zuc and Stup and Mojmilo? Were you able to -- to see and to recognise and to identify the force -- forces that were occupying those positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is impossible to answer that question. I wasn't able to see because it's just impossible. There were no insignia or anything, but from the wounded that came to the hospital, I knew where the lines were and I knew that Zuc was in the hands of BH army. Brejsto [phoen] Brdo, Sokolje, Mojmilo, Stup hill, Mount Igman, the part near Hrasnica that the Defence counsel referred to -- well, quite evidently, this was held by BH army. The Republika Srpska army held some slopes of the Zuc hill, but those were not dominating heights. So you could see the Zuc hill from the hospital, but I couldn't see the people who actually were manning those positions, and I was not interested in it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that the Republika Srpska Army also held some slopes of the Zuc hill, but they were not dominating. By that, what do you mean? Where were they in relation to the ABiH forces on Zuc and Stup and Mojmilo? Were they above or below, those forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I tried visualise this area, the lines held by the Republika Srpska army were not visible from Mojmilo, at Stup hill, they were on the slopes of Zuc facing north-west, not Sarajevo but north-west, Vogosca and the area facing Rajlovac municipality. So these were very low hills, as far as I know. I can't really make any claims because I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can't see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- enough of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to the rescue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm trying to, Your Honours, it seems like the whole map, which has a 65 ter number, wasn't uploaded, but my colleague, Ms. Bosnjakovic, is uploading it at this point if it can still help at that point. And that map, for everyone's information, is a map which shows the whole city of Sarajevo far to the north past Vogosca and to the south as well. It may help, but it's just a question of how long it takes for this exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While we wait for this I could perhaps just ask one question to the witness. Dr. Pejic, did you ever see artillery fire coming out of those hills? Was that possible for you or did you not witness -- did you not have time to witness any shelling coming out of those hills? If, for instance, you were looking towards Zuc or Mojmilo, did you ever see artillery fire coming from those --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- well, it would be quite brave to stand there and observe that. I had a different job. I was in the hospital. I was not outside, but according to the testimony of those who brought in the wounded, it was quite clear that the shells had come in from that area. 5.800 people in less than four years, you couldn't really observe that, but we gained indirect knowledge. We heard from the people telling us what happened once our job was done, then we asked questions. After all, my entire family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- lived there. I didn't come from Serbia; I was from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I appreciate the suffering that the Serbian people went through. I was just curious to know if you, yourself, had any chance to observe the firing. But thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it will take us long to find the map that we could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about some elevations that the Prosecutor pointed to you, the elevations that were in the Hrasnica area to the south-east. What did they look like in terms of their height and in relation to the location of the hospital and the positions facing Zuc and Hum?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: You mean the elevations that I indicated now or the elevations that have not been shown here that were controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, because we can't see them on the map.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the hospital, Ilidza, and this area, they were dominating heights, just like this elevation that was indicated by the Prosecutor were dominating in relation to -- to this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But they're closer to Mojmilo, Zuc, Hum --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That is the end of your evidence. We are grateful to you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness has been planned for tomorrow. This witness has serious health problems, and we thought that we -- that two witnesses planned for today would take up the whole of our session today. I hope that this witness will be in the condition to be heard tomorrow. We have three witnesses planned for tomorrow, but we didn't want to expose this witness, who has serious health problems, to having to wait here. And it was a big problem bringing him here at all. So I ask your leave to hear him tomorrow, and then to hear the other two witnesses planned for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In other words, we will adjourn now because you don't have another witness now? Well, in the circumstances, particularly in light of what you've said about the witness's health, the Chamber understands the position of the Defence. We'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 22nd day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
